evidence: Cic. Phil. 2.18: tenēsne memoriā praetextātum tē dēcoxisse? (Lewis & Short: “to become a bankrupt”)
Cic. Phil. 2.18; Cic. Cat. 2.3; Catull. 41.4 (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Fam. 9.16.7 (Lewis & Short s.v. cōpia: “to declare one’s self exempt through poverty”)

terms.gloss: insolvency (late legal Latin); first a boiling down
evidence: Cod. Just. 11.9.5: ūnīus dēcoctiōnī ūniversī respondēre cōgentur; cf. Cod. Theod. 4.9.3 (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Lewis & Short gives the word first of boiling down, in medical writers, and glosses the law codes’ use as “a decoction, mixture”; but there all are made answerable for one man’s dēcoctiō, which reads as his insolvency, the noun of dēcoquere, go bankrupt. Late, but with ancient warrant for Traupman’s sense.

sources: Lewis & Short: decoquo · Lewis & Short: decoctor · Lewis & Short: copia · Lewis & Short: decoctio
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 276.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
